beta to something a stranger can install. Update the status column as things
move; do not delete rows, so the history of what was decided stays readable.

## The decision everything else hangs on

**How are we distributing?** Still open, and it changes which rows below matter.

| Option | Cap | Review | Longevity |
|---|---|---|---|
| TestFlight external | 10,000 testers | Beta App Review | Builds expire every 90 days |
| Unlisted App Distribution | none | Full App Store review | Permanent, no discovery |
| Public listing | none | Full App Store review | Permanent |

If we stay on TestFlight, most of *Store listing* below is not required yet.
Everything in *Apple hard requirements* and *Our own bar* applies either way.

You cannot cap downloads on a normal listing. Any "limited release" has to come
from TestFlight's own cap or from being unlisted.

## Our own bar before strangers get in

Not Apple's rules — ours. See `world-release-blockers` in session memory.

| Item | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Per-household authorization | ✅ | Verified 2026-08-30 with a real outsider account: reads and writes both denied |
| Invite codes single-use, 10 min, 8 chars | ✅ | Tightened 2026-09-03 and deployed (Amplify job on `71cafb1`). Was 30 min / 6 chars. `regenerateInviteCodeFunction` was still generating with `Math.random()` — the live "Generate New Code" path — now `randomInt` from node:crypto. QR scanning added for in-person invites |
| Household required for every AI call | ✅ | Reject and allow paths both verified |
| AppSync request logging | ✅ | ERROR level, bodies excluded, 14-day retention; verified by generating denials |
| S3 enumeration closed | ✅ | `list` withheld; deployed policy confirmed |
| S3 per-household scoping | ⬜ | Unchanged. Anyone holding a key can still read or delete that file. Lambda broker is the fix, ~a day. See `s3-scoping-plan` |
| `inferProductAisle` store ownership | ✅ | Fixed 2026-09-03. The store read now projects `householdId` and rejects unless it is one of the caller's Cognito groups. The mappings read was also made serial after it — running them together meant another household's mappings were read before the check could reject, even though nothing reached the caller |
| `joinHousehold` rate limiting | 🚫 | Still deferred, and **less urgent than this file used to claim**. With 8-character single-use 10-minute codes, guessing is not the concern; burning Lambda invocations is, and a WAF rate rule is the answer to that, not a counter. The error-message half is done: invalid / expired / already-used now return one identical refusal, so a guesser is no longer told when they found a real code |
| Password floor above 6 chars | 🟡 | Raised to 8 with lowercase + number in `backend.ts` on 2026-09-03; **not yet deployed**. Symbols deliberately not required. Existing passwords keep working — Cognito validates on set. Verify against the pool after the Amplify job runs |
| Signup gating | ⬜ | Much less urgent now — a junk account costs a Cognito row and nothing else |

## To do: household lifecycle testing

A whole class of behaviour has never been exercised, because doing it properly
needs more than one throwaway account and a household that is safe to destroy.

**Set up a separate test household with two or three accounts.** Gmail
plus-addressing gives as many as needed — `mike.akram+t1@gmail.com`,
`+t2`, `+t3` — and codes land in the normal inbox. One creates a household, the
others join it with invite codes. Put a few items, a store and an aisle layout in
it so there is something to observe being kept or destroyed.

**Never point any of this at `TooFat&TooCurious`.** Everything below is
destructive, and there is one environment.

### Paths that have never been run

| Path | What it exercises | Verify |
|---|---|---|
| Member deletes their account, others remain | `detachUser`, group revoke, remaining count | Their items stay on the list; their Cognito group membership is gone; the household is intact; the other members can still read everything |
| **Last** member deletes their account | `deleteHouseholdData` cascade | Household, items, commits, stores, mappings and the Cognito group are all gone. Nothing orphaned |
| Owner removes a member | `remove`, which is owner-only | The removed person loses access immediately, not when their token expires |
| Owner leaves, others remain | The household with no owner | Remaining members can still use it; nobody can be removed any more, by design |
| Member leaves and rejoins | Colour reassignment, group re-grant | They do not collide with a colour someone took while they were away |
| Two people join on one code, racing | `consumeInviteCode` conditional write | Exactly one gets in; the other is told the code was used |

### Why it matters more than it looks

`deleteHouseholdData` is the most destructive code in the app and it is reached
by two different actions. It has only ever been observed through `leave`. The
reasoning "the account-deletion path reuses code that already works" is precisely
the reasoning that broke joining on 2026-08-31 — the code was fine, the IAM grant
around it was not.

The account-deletion path was verified on 2026-08-31 only for a user with **no**
household. That is the least interesting of the three branches.

## Moving the AI inside AWS

Worth exploring before public release. The motive is the privacy story and the
API keys, not cost.

**Where the calls are today:** seven Lambdas use Anthropic's SDK directly
(`parseIngredients`, `inferProductAisle`, `aisleExtractionJobHandler`,
`matchProductsToAisles`, `extractAislesFromImages`, `extractAisleMappings`,
`generateFullMappings`). Exactly one uses OpenAI, and it does nothing but
transcription.

### Claude → Bedrock: straightforward

| | |
|---|---|
| Effort | ~half a day. `@anthropic-ai/bedrock-sdk` keeps the same message shape, so the seven sites are largely an import and a model id |
| Wins | `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` disappears entirely — Bedrock authenticates with IAM, so there is no long-lived secret in SSM to leak or rotate. One vendor, one bill, same region |
| Check first | That `claude-haiku-4-5` and `claude-sonnet-4-6` are both available on Bedrock. New models land there later than the direct API |
| Watch | Bedrock per-token pricing differs. Prompt caching exists with different mechanics — currently moot at our volume, but do not assume it carries over unexamined |

### Whisper → somewhere in AWS: the harder half

Bedrock does not host Whisper. The options are Amazon Transcribe, or running a
speech model ourselves on SageMaker or ECS.

Neither is a swap. The current setup is tuned to Whisper's specific failure
modes: `gpt-4o-mini-transcribe` was chosen over `whisper-1` because the latter
completes trailing silence with YouTube caption boilerplate, and
`stripHallucinatedTail` exists to catch what still gets through. A different
engine has different failure modes and needs its own evaluation against real
dictation, not fixtures.

**How much is at stake, measured from CloudWatch on 2026-08-31:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Successful transcriptions, all time | 16 |
| Median transcript | 206 characters |
| Median latency | 3.2 s |
| Cost | Pennies. Not a reason to move |

So this is a disclosure decision, not an economic one. Moving Claude alone takes
the privacy policy from two external processors to one; the "AWS only" story
needs both, and transcription is the half with quality risk attached.

### Suggested order

1. Move Claude to Bedrock. Real security win, low risk, independent of everything else.
2. Evaluate Amazon Transcribe against real dictation separately, with the
   hallucination behaviour as the thing to measure. Only then decide whether the
   single-processor story is worth the change.

## What is deliberately not being built

- **Monetization.** Direction agreed — no feature gating, volume metered on
  trips, roughly \$0.99 to finish the month. Blocked on cost-per-household, which
  needs the Anthropic and OpenAI usage figures. AWS is \$3.19/month for the whole
  account, so those two numbers are the entire equation.
- **Ads.** Rejected. Sessions are seconds long and it is a shared family utility.
